bib.title: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Chapter 1: Introduction

question: What are the core concepts (curve fitting, probability, model selection, curse of dimensionality, decision theory, information theory) that underpin pattern recognition and machine learning?
contributions: Introduces over-fitting, regularization and model selection through polynomial curve fitting (1.1)
Introduces probability theory, Bayesian vs frequentist estimation, the Gaussian, MLE/MAP and Bayesian curve fitting (1.2)
Introduces model selection by validation, cross-validation and information criteria (1.3)
Introduces decision theory: misclassification rate, expected loss, reject option, generative/discriminative/discriminant approaches, regression loss functions (1.5)
Introduces entropy, KL divergence and mutual information (1.6)

results.claim: A degree-9 polynomial fitted by least squares to 10 noisy points passes through every point (zero training error) yet oscillates wildly and generalizes badly: over-fitting.
results.setup: Synthetic data: sin(2 pi x) plus Gaussian noise, N = 10 points with x spaced uniformly on [0,1]; polynomials of order M = 0, 1, 3, 9 fitted by sum-of-squares error (1.2).
results.quote: In fact, the polynomial passes exactly through each data point and E(w⋆) = 0.

results.claim: Test-set RMS error is small for orders 3 to 8 and large for low orders and for M = 9; test set has 100 points.
results.setup: Same synthetic problem; separate test set of 100 points generated by the same procedure with new noise (Fig 1.5). Values read from the figure, not tabulated.
results.quote: Values of M in the range 3 ⩽M ⩽8 give small values for the test set error
results.note: Figure 1.4 shows M = 0, 1, 3, 9 but Table 1.1 lists M = 0, 1, 6, 9; no M = 3 coefficients are printed.

results.claim: Least-squares coefficient magnitudes explode with polynomial order: for M = 9 the largest is about 1.06 million in absolute value, versus 0.82 and -1.27 at M = 1.
results.setup: Unregularized least squares on the N = 10 sinusoid data set, M = 9.
results.note: Table 1.2 repeats the same M = 9 unregularized column (ln lambda = -inf).

results.claim: Adding a quadratic penalty with ln lambda = -18 shrinks the M = 9 coefficients (largest magnitude about 91.5 instead of about 1.06 million) and suppresses over-fitting; ln lambda = 0 over-shrinks and fits poorly again.
results.setup: M = 9 polynomial on N = 10 sinusoid data, regularized error (1.4), ln lambda in {-inf, -18, 0}.
results.table: Table 1.2, row w*_8, column ln lambda = -18
results.note: Largest magnitude in the ln lambda = -18 column is -91.53 (w*_8), not w*_9 = 72.68.

results.claim: With the same M = 9 model, increasing the data set from 15 to 100 points reduces over-fitting.
results.setup: M = 9 polynomial, unregularized sum-of-squares, N = 15 and N = 100 (Fig 1.6). Qualitative, from the plots.
results.quote: We see that, for a given model complexity, the over-ﬁtting problem become less severe as the size of the data set increases.
results.note: The quoted sentence contains the printed typo 'become' and the ligature 'ﬁ'.

results.claim: Rule of thumb that the number of data points should be at least 5 or 10 times the number of adaptive parameters; the book immediately says parameter count is not the right complexity measure.
results.setup: Heuristic stated for fitting models of limited complexity to a data set; no experiment.
results.quote: no less than some multiple (say 5 or 10) of the number of adaptive parameters in the model

results.claim: Regularized least squares equals MAP estimation under a Gaussian prior on w with precision alpha and Gaussian noise precision beta, with lambda = alpha/beta.
results.setup: Polynomial model (1.1), Gaussian noise (1.60), prior p(w|alpha) = N(w|0, alpha^-1 I) (1.65); derivation in Sec 1.2.5.
results.quote: with a regularization parameter given by λ = α/β.

results.claim: Maximum-likelihood variance of a Gaussian is biased low by the factor (N-1)/N; dividing by N-1 gives an unbiased estimate.
results.setup: N i.i.d. univariate Gaussian observations with unknown mean and variance; derivation left to Exercise 1.12.
results.quote: so that on average the maximum likelihood estimate will obtain the correct mean but will underestimate the true variance by a factor (N −1)/N.

results.claim: Bayesian curve fitting gives a Gaussian predictive distribution whose variance is beta^-1 + phi(x)^T S phi(x), so uncertainty depends on x. Illustrated with M = 9, alpha = 5e-3, beta = 11.1.
results.setup: M = 9 polynomial on the sinusoid data; alpha and beta fixed, beta equal to the known noise precision.
results.quote: α = 5 × 10−3 and β = 11.1 (corresponding to the known noise variance)
results.note: Eq. 1.72 prints S^-1 = alpha I + beta sum phi(x_n) phi(x)^T, with phi(x) not phi(x_n) in the second factor; this is a printed typo, the sum should be over phi(x_n) phi(x_n)^T.

results.claim: Maximum likelihood on a coin tossed 3 times with 3 heads gives probability of heads of 1, which a Bayesian with any reasonable prior avoids.
results.setup: Fair-looking coin, 3 tosses, all heads; no prior numbers given.
results.quote: A classical maximum likelihood estimate of the probability of landing heads would give 1, implying that all future tosses will land

results.claim: Boxes-of-fruit example: overall probability of drawing an apple is 11/20.
results.setup: Red box 2 apples and 6 oranges, blue box 3 apples and 1 orange; red chosen with probability 4/10, blue 6/10; fruit replaced after each draw.
results.note: Quote is the PDF text-layer flattening of the fractions in eq. 1.22.

results.claim: Given an orange, the posterior probability the box was red is 2/3 although the prior of red was 4/10: evidence outweighs the prior.
results.setup: Same boxes-of-fruit setup, Bayes' theorem (1.23).
results.quote: we ﬁnd that the posterior probability of the red box is now 2/3

results.claim: S-fold cross-validation uses (S-1)/S of the data for training in each run, at a cost of S times as many training runs; S = N gives leave-one-out.
results.setup: Illustrated for S = 4 (Fig 1.18).
results.quote: This allows a proportion (S −1)/S of the available data to be used for training

results.claim: With several complexity hyperparameters, grid search over validation runs may need a number of runs exponential in the number of parameters.
results.setup: Cross-validation or hold-out with multiple regularization parameters per model; worst case, no experiment.
results.quote: could, in the worst case, require a number of training runs that is exponential in the number of parameters

results.claim: AIC chooses the model maximising ln p(D|w_ML) - M (M = number of adjustable parameters); the book says such criteria tend to favour overly simple models.
results.setup: Model comparison with maximum-likelihood fits (Akaike 1974); BIC deferred to Sec 4.4.1.
results.quote: ln p(D|wML) −M (1.73)
results.note: Printed with the larger-is-better sign convention (log-likelihood minus M), not the usual 2M - 2 ln L form.

results.claim: Grid cells grow exponentially with input dimension D; a cubic polynomial in D variables has coefficients growing like D^3, and order M like D^M.
results.setup: General polynomial of order M in D inputs (1.74); Exercise 1.16 asks for N(D,M) = (D+M)!/(D! M!) and the D = 10, D = 100, M = 3 counts (not computed in the text).
results.quote: For a polynomial of order M, the growth in the number of coefﬁcients is like DM.

results.claim: In D dimensions the fraction of a unit sphere's volume in the shell between 1-eps and 1 is 1-(1-eps)^D, which tends to 1 for large D even for small eps.
results.setup: Sphere of radius 1, D = 1, 2, 5, 20 plotted in Fig 1.22.

results.claim: In the oil-flow illustration, inputs are 12-dimensional gamma-ray densitometer measurements and only 100 points over two inputs (x6, x7) are shown.
results.setup: Synthetic pipeline data (Bishop and James, 1993): oil, water, gas in three geometrical configurations (homogenous, annular, laminar); 3 classes.
results.quote: Each data point comprises a 12-dimensional input vector

results.claim: Minimum misclassification rate is achieved by assigning each x to the class with the largest posterior p(Ck|x).
results.setup: Derived for two classes (1.78) and K classes (1.79); Fig 1.24.
results.quote: we see that each x should be assigned to the class having the largest posterior probability p(Ck|x).

results.claim: With the cancer loss matrix (loss 1000 for a missed cancer, 1 for a false alarm, 0 otherwise), the minimum expected-loss rule assigns x to the class j that minimizes sum_k L_kj p(Ck|x).
results.setup: Two-class medical diagnosis, Fig 1.25; rows true class, columns assigned class.
results.quote: there is a loss of 1000 if a patient having cancer is diagnosed as healthy.

results.claim: Reject option: reject inputs whose largest posterior is <= theta; theta = 1 rejects everything, theta < 1/K rejects nothing.
results.setup: K-class classification with posterior probabilities.
results.quote: if there are K classes then setting θ < 1/K will ensure that no examples are rejected.

results.claim: With a rare class (1 in 1,000 are cancer), a classifier that labels everything normal scores 99.9% accuracy; balance the training set and correct the posteriors by dividing by the training class fractions, multiplying by the population fractions and renormalizing.
results.setup: Hypothetical X-ray screening set; prior correction only works with posterior-probability models, not discriminant functions.
results.quote: a classiﬁer that assigned every point to the normal class would already achieve 99.9% accuracy

results.claim: The three decision approaches rank in decreasing complexity: (a) generative (model p(x|Ck) and p(Ck)), (b) discriminative (model p(Ck|x)), (c) discriminant function with no probabilities.
results.setup: Classification (Sec 1.5.4) and regression (Sec 1.5.5).
results.quote: These are given, in decreasing order of complexity, by:

results.claim: Squared loss is minimized by the conditional mean E[t|x]; the minimum expected loss is the noise variance of t, which is irreducible.
results.setup: Flexible y(x), calculus of variations (1.88-1.90).
results.quote: Because it is independent of y(x), it represents the irreducible minimum value of the loss function.

results.claim: Minkowski loss |y-t|^q is minimized by the conditional mean for q = 2, the conditional median for q = 1 and the conditional mode for q -> 0.
results.setup: Expected Lq loss (1.91), Fig 1.29 plots q = 0.3, 1, 2, 10; proof in Exercise 1.27.
results.quote: The minimum of E[Lq] is given by the conditional mean for q = 2, the conditional median for q = 1, and the conditional mode for q →0.

results.claim: Entropy of 8 equally likely states is 3 bits; the non-uniform example (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/64 x4) has entropy 2 bits, achieved exactly by the code 0, 10, 110, 1110, 111100, 111101, 111110, 111111.
results.setup: Example from Cover and Thomas (1991); 8 states a..h.
results.quote: The entropy in this case is given by
results.note: The number 2 bits appears in the text lines that follow (H[x] = ... = 2 bits and average code length = ... = 2 bits).

results.claim: The uniform distribution over 30 bins has maximum entropy ln 30 = 3.40 nats; the two example histograms have H = 1.77 and H = 3.09.
results.setup: Histograms over 30 bins, Fig 1.30.
results.quote: The largest entropy would arise from a uniform distribution that would give H = −ln(1/30) = 3.40.

results.claim: Among densities with given mean and variance, the Gaussian maximizes differential entropy, which equals (1/2)(1+ln(2 pi sigma^2)) and is negative for sigma^2 < 1/(2 pi e).
results.setup: Constrained maximization with Lagrange multipliers (1.105-1.110); Exercises 1.34-1.35.
results.quote: because H(x) < 0 in (1.110) for σ2 < 1/(2πe).

results.claim: KL(p||q) >= 0 with equality iff p = q (via Jensen); it is asymmetric; minimizing KL(p||q(.|theta)) on a sample is equivalent to maximum likelihood.
results.setup: Eqs 1.113-1.119; p unknown, approximated by a sum over training points via (1.35).
results.quote: Thus we see that minimizing this Kullback-Leibler divergence is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood function.
results.note: Eq. 1.119 prints the sample approximation as an unscaled sum, whereas (1.35) has a factor 1/N; the omitted constant does not change the argmin.

results.claim: Mutual information is KL between the joint and the product of marginals, is >= 0 with equality iff independent, and equals H[x] - H[x|y] = H[y] - H[y|x].
results.setup: Eqs 1.120-1.121; Exercise 1.41; Exercise 1.39 asks for I on the joint of Table 1.3.

limits: Chapter is informal and deliberately introductory; derivations are pushed to exercises (e.g. unbiased variance, Gaussian entropy) or later chapters (Bayesian posterior for curve fitting in Sec 3.3, Bayesian model comparison in Sec 3.4).

All empirical content is synthetic: the sin(2 pi x) data set (N = 10, 15, 100; test set 100) and the 12-dimensional oil-flow data; no real-data benchmarks, no seeds, and noise level not stated in the chapter (Appendix A, not included; Fig 1.17 gives beta = 11.1 as the known noise precision).
Figures give the curve-fitting results (Figs 1.4-1.8); only the coefficient tables 1.1 and 1.2 print numbers, so train/test RMS values are not recoverable from the text.
The chapter shows the 5x or 10x rule of thumb only as a heuristic and says the parameter count is not the right complexity measure (Chapter 3).

AIC is stated in its older log-likelihood minus M form; the book itself notes such criteria favour overly simple models. Dated: the book's statement that Monte Carlo methods have 'mainly been used for small-scale problems' and that variational Bayes/EP enable large-scale use reflects 2006; deep learning is not mentioned.
Reinforcement learning is treated only as one paragraph; the book says a detailed treatment is beyond its scope.

Frequentist vs Bayesian: the book states a Bayesian emphasis and concedes that priors are often chosen for convenience and that poor priors can give poor results with high confidence, so cross-validation remains useful (p. 23).
practices: Fit the model by minimizing sum-of-squares, and choose model complexity (M or lambda) on a separate validation (hold-out) set rather than on training error (Sec 1.1, p. 11).
Use a regularizer (ridge/weight decay) to control over-fitting in flexible models, and omit or separately regularize the bias coefficient w0 (Sec 1.1, p. 10).
Pre-process test data with exactly the same steps as the training data (Sec 1, p. 2).
Pre-processing discards information, so take care it does not remove information needed for the task (Sec 1, p. 3).
Keep a third test set for the final assessment if model design is iterated many times on a limited validation set (Sec 1.3, p. 32).
Use S-fold cross-validation when data is limited; S = N (leave-one-out) when data is particularly scarce; expect S times the training cost (Sec 1.3, p. 32-33).
Work with log-likelihoods: the sum of log probabilities avoids numerical underflow of a product of small probabilities (Sec 1.2.4, p. 26).
Use the unbiased variance estimate with N-1 in the denominator for small N (Sec 1.2.4, p. 27).

For classification, model posterior probabilities rather than only a discriminant function, so loss matrices, reject thresholds, class priors and model combination can be changed without retraining (Sec 1.5.4, p. 44-45).
For imbalanced classes, train on a balanced set and correct posteriors by dividing by training class fractions, multiplying by population fractions and renormalizing (Sec 1.5.4, p. 45).
Choose the loss to match the costs of errors (e.g. 1000 vs 1) instead of using misclassification rate alone (Sec 1.5.2, p. 41).
Use a reject option and defer ambiguous inputs to a human expert (Sec 1.5.3, p. 42).
Do not trust low-dimensional geometric intuition in high dimensions; rely on low effective dimensionality and local smoothness (Sec 1.4, p. 36-37).
Minimizing KL to the data distribution is the same as maximum likelihood; negative log likelihood is the error function (Sec 1.2.3 and 1.6.1, p. 23, 57).

terms.definition: the automatic discovery of regularities in data through the use of computer algorithms and with the use of these regularities to take actions such as classifying the data into different categories
The ability to categorize correctly new examples that differ from those used for training
pre-processing stage in which input variables are transformed into a new space of variables where the problem is hoped to be easier
training data comprises examples of the input vectors along with their corresponding target vectors
classification assigns each input to one of a finite number of discrete categories; regression has one or more continuous outputs
training data consists of input vectors without target values: clustering, density estimation, or projection for visualization
finding suitable actions in a given situation to maximize a reward, by trial and error, with credit assignment and an exploration/exploitation trade-off
a high-order polynomial gives an excellent fit to the training data but the fitted curve oscillates wildly and is a poor representation of the generating function
E_RMS = sqrt(2 E(w*) / N), measured on the same scale and in the same units as the target variable

terms.term: regularization / shrinkage / ridge regression / weight decay
terms.definition: adding a penalty term to the error function to discourage large coefficients; the quadratic penalty is ridge regression in statistics and weight decay in neural networks
separate data used to optimize model complexity (M or lambda)
p(X) = sum_Y p(X,Y); p(X,Y) = p(Y|X) p(X)
p(Y|X) = p(X|Y) p(Y) / p(X)
prior is the probability available before observing the evidence; posterior is the probability after observing it
p(D|w) viewed as a function of the parameter vector w; not a probability distribution over w
p(x) such that the probability of x in (x, x+dx) is p(x) dx for dx -> 0
data points drawn independently from the same distribution
frequentist estimator setting w to the value that maximizes p(D|w); the negative log likelihood is called an error function
create L data sets of size N by drawing N points with replacement from the original set, then examine variability of estimates across them
systematic underestimation of the variance by factor (N-1)/N
reciprocal of the variance, beta = 1/sigma^2
variables such as alpha that control the distribution of model parameters
determining w by maximizing the posterior distribution
probability distribution over t for a new x, rather than a point estimate
partition data into S groups, train on S-1 and test on the held-out group, repeat for all S and average; S = N gives leave-one-out
difficulties that arise in spaces of many dimensions, e.g. the number of grid cells grows exponentially with D
regions Rk of input space assigned to class Ck, and the boundaries between them
a single, overall measure of loss incurred in taking any of the available decisions; L_kj is the loss for assigning true class Ck to Cj
avoiding decisions on difficult cases by rejecting inputs whose largest posterior is <= theta

terms.term: generative model / discriminative model / discriminant function
terms.definition: generative models model the distribution of inputs as well as outputs; discriminative models model the posteriors directly; a discriminant function maps inputs directly to class labels
detecting new data points with low p(x), for which predictions may be of low accuracy
p(xI, xB | Ck) = p(xI|Ck) p(xB|Ck)
the conditional average y(x) = E_t[t|x], the minimizer of expected squared loss
E[Lq] = integral |y(x) - t|^q p(x,t) dx dt
H[x] = -sum_x p(x) log2 p(x), the average amount of information transmitted; lower bound on bits needed (noiseless coding theorem, Shannon 1948)
H[x] = -integral p(x) ln p(x) dx for continuous variables
H[y|x] = -integral p(y,x) ln p(y|x) dy dx; H[x,y] = H[y|x] + H[x]
KL(p||q) = -integral p(x) ln (q(x)/p(x)) dx, the average additional information needed when q is used instead of the true p
for convex f, f(E[x]) <= E[f(x)]
I[x,y] = KL(p(x,y) || p(x)p(y))
chooses the model for which ln p(D|wML) - M is largest, M = number of adjustable parameters

figures.caption: Plots of polynomials having various orders M, shown as red curves, ﬁtted to the data set shown in Figure 1.2.
figures.why: Shows under-fit (M=0,1), good fit (M=3) and over-fit (M=9) side by side.

figures.caption: Graphs of the root-mean-square error, deﬁned by (1.3), evaluated on the training set and on an independent test set for various values of M.
figures.why: The canonical train-versus-test error U-curve against model complexity.

figures.caption: Plots of the solutions obtained by minimizing the sum-of-squares error function using the M = 9 polynomial for N = 15 data points (left plot) and N = 100 data points (right plot).
figures.why: More data reduces over-fitting for fixed complexity.

figures.caption: M = 9 polynomials fitted with regularized error (1.4) for ln lambda = -18 and ln lambda = 0; RMS error versus ln lambda.
figures.why: Shows lambda acting as a complexity knob, with the same U-shape against ln lambda.

figures.caption: Coefficients w* for polynomials of various order; coefficients for M = 9 with various values of lambda.
figures.why: Numbers that make coefficient explosion and shrinkage concrete.

figures.caption: Illustration of how bias arises in using maximum likelihood to determine the variance of a Gaussian.
figures.why: Three 2-point samples show why variance measured about the sample mean is too small.

figures.caption: The predictive distribution resulting from a Bayesian treatment of polynomial curve fitting using an M = 9 polynomial, with the fixed parameters alpha = 5e-3 and beta = 11.1.
figures.why: Predictive uncertainty band that widens away from the data.

figures.caption: The technique of S-fold cross-validation, illustrated here for the case of S = 4.
figures.why: Layout of the held-out blocks across the S runs.

figures.caption: Grid cells growing exponentially with D; fraction of sphere volume in the outer shell; Gaussian density versus radius for D = 1, 2, 20.
Schematic illustration of the joint probabilities p(x, Ck) for each of two classes plotted against x, together with the decision boundary.
figures.why: Shows why the posterior-maximizing boundary removes the red error region.

figures.caption: Loss matrix for the cancer problem; illustration of the reject option.
figures.why: Asymmetric costs and the reject band in one picture each.

figures.caption: Class-conditional densities for two classes (left) with the corresponding posteriors (right).
figures.why: Why modelling p(x|Ck) can be wasteful when only p(Ck|x) is needed.

figures.caption: Regression function as the conditional mean; plots of |y-t|^q for q = 0.3, 1, 2, 10.
figures.why: Links loss function choice to mean, median and mode.

figures.caption: Histograms over 30 bins with H = 1.77 and H = 3.09; a convex function with its chord.
figures.why: Entropy as spread; geometric picture behind Jensen's inequality.

problems: No embedded instructions found in the PDF text.
Extraction is the plain text layer: equations are flattened and symbols are scattered over lines; ligatures (fi, fl) appear as single glyphs in quotes.

Printed typos in the book kept as found: eq. 1.72 uses phi(x)^T in the second factor of the sum; eq. 1.119 omits the 1/N from (1.35); Exercise 1.34 says the stationary point of functional (1.108) 'is given by (1.108)' (circular reference); Exercise 1.16 contains the garbled 'M6th'; the text reads 'become less severe' on p. 9.
Entropy is defined with log2 (1.93) but the next remark and the rest of the chapter use ln ('p ln p'); the book announces the switch to nats on p. 50.
Table 1.1 lists M = 0, 1, 6, 9 while Figure 1.4 plots M = 0, 1, 3, 9, so there are no printed coefficients for the M = 3 curve the text calls best.
